Artificial Intelligence Basics

Sample knowledge document for testing document-based question answering

Purpose

This document contains deliberately specific facts and examples. Upload it to your RAG application, then ask the sample questions to check whether retrieval finds the right passages and whether answers include source references.

1. Artificial intelligence

Artificial intelligence is a field of computing focused on building systems that perform tasks commonly associated with human intelligence, such as perception, language understanding, reasoning, and decision support.

AI is a broad field. Machine learning is a subset of AI in which systems learn patterns from data rather than relying only on explicitly written rules.

Deep learning is a subset of machine learning that uses neural networks with multiple layers to learn complex patterns.

2. Machine learning approaches

Supervised learning trains a model using examples that include input data and known target labels or values. Classification predicts categories, while regression predicts numerical values.

Unsupervised learning works with data that does not have target labels. Clustering groups similar examples, while dimensionality reduction represents data with fewer variables.

Reinforcement learning trains an agent through interaction with an environment. The agent receives rewards or penalties and learns a policy for choosing actions.

3. Neural networks

A neural network is made of connected computational units often called neurons. Common layers include an input layer, one or more hidden layers, and an output layer.

Training adjusts model parameters to reduce a loss function. Backpropagation calculates gradients, and an optimizer uses those gradients to update parameters.

Overfitting occurs when a model performs well on training data but poorly on new data. Validation data, regularization, and early stopping can help reduce overfitting.

4. Generative AI and language models

Generative AI creates new content such as text, images, audio, or code based on patterns learned during training.

A large language model generates text by predicting likely next tokens based on the preceding context. Its output can sound confident while still being incorrect.

Retrieval-augmented generation combines information retrieval with language generation. It retrieves relevant external information and supplies it as context to a language model.

5. Quick facts for question testing

Machine learning is a subset of artificial intelligence.

Deep learning is a subset of machine learning.

Classification predicts categories; regression predicts numerical values.

Overfitting means poor generalization to unseen data.

RAG grounds generation with retrieved information.

Suggested test questions

Ask these questions in your RAG chat after uploading this PDF. Compare the answer with the information in the document and inspect the cited page or chunk.

• What is the relationship between AI, machine learning, and deep learning?

• What is the difference between classification and regression?

• How does reinforcement learning work?

• What is overfitting and how can it be reduced?

• Explain retrieval-augmented generation in simple terms.

Purpose

1. Dataset preparation

A dataset is a collection of examples used to analyze a problem or train and evaluate a model. Each example may contain features and, in supervised learning, a target label.

Data cleaning can include handling missing values, removing duplicates, correcting inconsistent formats, and checking for outliers.

Data leakage occurs when information unavailable at prediction time improperly enters model training or evaluation. Leakage can make evaluation results look better than real-world performance.

2. Training and evaluation

A training set is used to fit model parameters. A validation set helps select models and tune hyperparameters. A test set is held back for a final estimate of performance.

Accuracy is the proportion of predictions that are correct. Precision is the proportion of predicted positives that are truly positive. Recall is the proportion of actual positives that are identified.

The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall. It is useful when both false positives and false negatives matter.

3. Model evaluation example

Suppose a classifier makes 100 predictions. It correctly identifies 36 positive cases, incorrectly labels 9 negative cases as positive, and misses 4 positive cases.

In this example, true positives equal 36, false positives equal 9, and false negatives equal 4.

Precision is 36 divided by 45, which equals 0.80 or 80 percent. Recall is 36 divided by 40, which equals 0.90 or 90 percent.

The F1 score is 2 multiplied by precision multiplied by recall, divided by precision plus recall. With precision 0.80 and recall 0.90, the F1 score is approximately 0.847 or 84.7 percent.

4. Model improvement

Cross-validation evaluates a model across multiple train-validation splits. It can provide a more stable estimate than relying on a single split.

Regularization discourages overly complex models. Examples include L1 and L2 penalties.

A confusion matrix summarizes predicted and actual classes using true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives.

5. Quick facts for question testing

Training data fits model parameters; validation data supports model selection; test data estimates final performance.

Precision measures the reliability of positive predictions.

Recall measures how many actual positive cases are found.

F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall.

Data leakage can produce misleadingly optimistic evaluation results.

Suggested test questions

Ask these questions in your RAG chat after uploading this PDF. Compare the answer with the information in the document and inspect the cited page or chunk.

• What is data leakage?

• What is the purpose of a validation set?

• Using the example in this document, calculate precision and recall.

• What does the F1 score combine?

• How does a confusion matrix help evaluate a classifier?

Cybersecurity Fundamentals

Purpose

1. What is cybersecurity?

Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting computers, networks, applications, and data from unauthorized access, disruption, damage, or theft.

The three core security objectives are confidentiality, integrity, and availability. This model is commonly called the CIA triad.

Confidentiality means information is accessible only to authorized people. Integrity means information remains accurate and has not been improperly changed. Availability means systems and information are accessible when needed.

2. Common cyberattacks

Phishing is a social-engineering attack in which an attacker uses deceptive messages or websites to trick people into revealing information or installing malware.

A denial-of-service attack attempts to make a service unavailable by overwhelming it with traffic or requests. A distributed denial-of-service attack uses many systems to generate the traffic.

A brute-force attack repeatedly tries passwords or keys until the correct one is found. Rate limiting, multi-factor authentication, and strong unique passwords reduce this risk.

Ransomware is malware that blocks access to data, often by encrypting files, and demands payment. Offline backups and tested recovery procedures help reduce its impact.

3. Security controls

Multi-factor authentication requires two or more different categories of evidence, such as something a person knows, has, or is.

A firewall filters network traffic according to a defined security policy. It can allow or block traffic based on rules such as source, destination, protocol, and port.

Encryption transforms readable information into ciphertext so that it cannot be understood without the appropriate key. Encryption protects data in transit and at rest.

The principle of least privilege gives each user or service only the permissions needed to perform its task.

4. Incident response

A basic incident response lifecycle includes preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery, and lessons learned.

4. Incident response

Containment limits the spread or impact of an incident. Eradication removes the cause, such as malware or compromised accounts. Recovery restores normal operations and verifies that systems are safe.

Organizations should preserve relevant logs and evidence, document decisions, and communicate through an established incident response process.

5. Quick facts for question testing

The CIA triad consists of confidentiality, integrity, and availability.

Phishing relies on deception and social engineering.

MFA uses at least two different authentication factor categories.

A firewall enforces network traffic rules.

Offline backups can help an organization recover from ransomware.

Suggested test questions

Ask these questions in your RAG chat after uploading this PDF. Compare the answer with the information in the document and inspect the cited page or chunk.

• What are the three parts of the CIA triad?

• How is a DDoS attack different from a regular DoS attack?

• Name three ways to reduce brute-force password attacks.

• What is the difference between containment and eradication?

• Why are offline backups useful against ransomware?
